summary: The build can start: all runtime and DocumentDB data‑plane tools required by the sample are present (python, pip, the documentdb MCP server and many DocumentDB skills, az CLI). Key factual confusions in the cold answers were identified and corrected (resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; CLI uses az documentdb; billing is vCore/compute-tier, not RU/s; integrated vector and full‑text search exist, etc.). Missing/lacking items are mostly non-blocking (mongosh is not on PATH; azd/bicep/terraform/dotnet are absent but not required). There are a few information gaps (LangChain tool-wrapper examples, explicit sample schema and LLM model choice) the implementer must decide before coding.
summary_points: All essential runtime tools for this Python LangChain + DocumentDB sample are present: python, pip, az, docker, node, the documentdb MCP server, and the DocumentDB skills.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated: this service uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and az documentdb CLI commands; it bills by vCore (cluster tier), not RUs; it supports integrated vector search (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) and an integrated full‑text $search engine.

The build is ready to start but with small gaps: mongosh is not installed (use MCP server tools as a workaround), and the sample needs explicit choices the prompt left open (LangChain model/provider, exact document schema, and prompt template).
Inventory additions are optional: install mongosh for convenient manual inspection; azd, bicep, terraform and dotnet are not necessary for this sample.

Concrete guidance and sources are provided for each incorrect cold answer so the implementer won't adopt the wrong assumptions that would break the app (wrong CLI, wrong resource types, wrong connection string shape, wrong billing model).

tools.workaround: Install Python 3.10+ (the sample assumes a modern Python 3.x). Use the system package manager or pyenv; the agent kit README should document a supported Python version.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for accounts: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB / DocumentDB account resource). For sub-resources the type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbResources or databaseAccounts/containers for SQL API, but the top-level cluster/account is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are represented by the Microsoft.DocumentDB resource provider using the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (sometimes shown as `mongoclusters`).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM / Terraform docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB APIs and documentation use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and nested mongodbDatabases resources for the Cosmos DB (RU) MongoDB API. The service rename and new vCore offering use a distinct top-level resource type (mongoclusters), so the two resource-models coexist in docs.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts instead of Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in IaC or az commands, any deployment or resource queries for the vCore clusters would fail or target the wrong service. The sample must use the mongoclusters resource type when referencing the vCore cluster.
improvements: On the Quickstart: Deploy page, add a single note that distinguishes the earlier Cosmos 'databaseAccounts' model from the newer vCore 'mongoclusters' resource and link to the migration or naming FAQ.
Update the documentdb MCP skill description to state it targets Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters explicitly (so agent tooling prefers that resource type).

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create an account for MongoDB API: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session --kind MongoDB
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore DocumentDB cluster is managed with the az documentdb CLI command group (az documentdb mongocluster ...). The documentdb extension is used for the documentdb command group; examples use az documentdb mongocluster create/list/show.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB (the databaseAccounts resource) used az cosmosdb or az cosmosdb mongodb subcommands. The new vCore offering is surfaced under az documentdb (mongocluster) which is a separate command group/extension.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure Cosmos DB account (older Cosmos docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb to manage vCore clusters would not find or manage mongoclusters; scripts and automation would fail. Use az documentdb mongocluster commands for cluster management.
improvements: Add a brief cross-reference in the az cosmosdb docs and in the 'create cluster' quickstart that points to az documentdb for vCore clusters and explains the difference.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@{apiVersion}' (for example @2021-04-15). Terraform (AzRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account. Example Terraform resource: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { ... }
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore Azure DocumentDB clusters you should use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource in ARM/Bicep or the AzAPI/Azure provider equivalent (examples and Terraform AzAPI samples target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters / mongoclusters). The older databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases resource still exists for Cosmos DB (RU) but is not the vCore cluster resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM / Terraform docs)
Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases (ARM docs) - older model

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB API used databaseAccounts and azurerm_cosmosdb_account; the vCore DocumentDB product uses a distinct top-level resource (mongoclusters). The coexistence of both resource families in docs causes confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Terraform resource type would prevent creating or targeting the intended vCore cluster from IaC. Use mongoclusters in Bicep/ARM and the AzAPI terraform resource examples shown for mongoclusters.
improvements: Add an explicit 'deploying vCore clusters' section to the Bicep/Terraform quickstarts demonstrating Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters with exact API versions and a Terraform AzAPI snippet.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB-style connection string. Typical form (non-SRV): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Username is often in the form <dbUser>@<account>. Use TLS/SSL (ssl=true or tls=true). Some drivers accept mongodb+srv if DNS SRV is provided, but Cosmos Mongo API historically requires the explicit host:port (10255) with ssl enabled.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters the connection string commonly uses the mongodb+srv scheme and the cluster-specific host suffix like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (SRV), or explicit hostnames/ports where applicable; the CLI and management docs show commands such as az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings and examples using mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID OIDC flows. The older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) Mongo API used hostnames like <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255; that pattern is for the RU-based Cosmos accounts and differs from the new mongocluster hostnames.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings (CLI quickstart)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed connection-string details for the older Cosmos DB Mongo API (host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255, commonly seen in Cosmos RU docs) with the newer vCore DocumentDB clusters that present SRV hostnames under global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and support SRV and passwordless OIDC forms.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (older Cosmos docs, shows :10255)

confusions.build_risk: Using the old host suffix/port (10255) or wrong SRV form may cause connection failures for vCore clusters (wrong hostname or incompatible auth mechanism). The sample must read the exact connection string from the environment (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and use the MCP 'list-connection-strings' or the portal to obtain the canonical value.
improvements: Add a short 'Connection string shapes' section to the 'how-to-connect' doc that enumerates the SRV form for mongoclusters and the legacy :10255 form for Cosmos RU accounts and says which one the agent should expect in DOCUMENTDB_URI.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is billed primarily by Request Units (RUs/sec) for provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale). There is also a serverless option and lately dedicated vCore-based SKUs for some Cosmos APIs in preview/GA, but the common model for Cosmos/Mongo API is RU-based provisioned throughput or serverless. Expect RU/s billing for collection throughput.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute (cluster tier in vCores and memory per shard) and storage. It does not bill per-request RUs for the vCore product; request units are the billing model for Cosmos DB's RU-based accounts. DocumentDB uses M-series tiers (M10, M20, M30, etc.) for compute and per‑GiB storage pricing.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Compute and storage configurations for Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the Cosmos RU model (RUs) which applies to Cosmos DB's RU-based accounts. The newer vCore DocumentDB offering is vCore/compute-tier billed and intentionally differs from RU billing.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB billing (RU model) references

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based capacity, they may attempt to set throughput on collections in the wrong way or choose an architecture that breaks cost/scale expectations. Use vCore tiers (M30 etc.) when sizing and cost estimation.
improvements: Add a short billing comparison tile on the product overview page clarifying that vCore DocumentDB uses cluster-tier billing and that Cosmos DB RU-based accounts are distinct.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary method for MongoDB API is username/password (MongoDB credentials mapped to Cosmos account keys) using the account key as password (username often <dbUser>@<account>). Cosmos DB also supports resource tokens and Azure RBAC/Entra ID for management plane and, more recently, data plane RBAC for some APIs. For Entra ID data-plane auth for Mongo API you obtain an Azure AD access token (via MSAL/Azure Identity) and then use the provider-specific connection method (if supported). Historically MongoDB drivers authenticate with the Mongo-style username/password; Entra ID data-plane auth for Mongo API is limited or requires special preview features — so in practice use the Mongo credentials from the account or created database users.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports NativeAuth (username/password) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) for data-plane authentication. You can enable Microsoft Entra ID on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes includes MicrosoftEntraID) and connect via OIDC by using mongodb+srv with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC, or drivers' OIDC callback/token approaches (examples exist for pymongo using an OIDC callback that obtains tokens from DefaultAzureCredential).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged because older Cosmos DB Mongo API had limited Entra ID support; the vCore DocumentDB product actively supports Microsoft Entra ID with documented connection string forms (MONGODB-OIDC).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is not supported, they may hardcode username/password secrets. Conversely, assuming Entra ID without enabling authConfig or provisioning identities will cause authentication failures. The sample should read DOCUMENTDB_URI and support either mode; provide instructions for enabling MicrosoftEntraID on the cluster when demonstrating OIDC.
improvements: Add an example in the Quickstart that shows both a SCRAM (username/password) and a Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) pymongo connect snippet, and show the CLI or portal steps to enable authConfig.allowedModes.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For application data access using the MongoDB API, use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., pymongo for Python, mongodb for Node). There is a service-specific management SDK (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / azure-cosmos for SQL API) for control-plane tasks, but for application reads/writes use the vanilla MongoDB driver rather than an Azure-specific data SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo in Python). Management/control‑plane tasks use Azure control-plane SDKs, but application read/writes use normal MongoDB drivers. The Learn quickstarts and examples use pymongo and show how to use OIDC callbacks for Entra ID when needed.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python
Build a Python console app with Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: As I understand Azure Cosmos DB / DocumentDB does not currently provide native vector index primitives like HNSW/IVF/DiskANN via the MongoDB API. There is no standard createIndex() variant to create a vector index in Cosmos DB today. If vector search is required you generally either: 1) use an external vector-search service (Azure Cognitive Search/custom indexer or an external vector engine) or 2) use MongoDB Atlas which supports vector indexes. Therefore there is no Cosmos-specific create command for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect — Azure DocumentDB supports integrated vector indexes and multiple algorithms (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann). You create them using createIndex/createIndexes with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions or the documented vector-index JSON. The docs include examples for vector-ivf, vector-hnsw and DiskANN and show how to use the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch) to run vector queries.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (DiskANN / HNSW / IVF examples)
Quickstart: Use vector search with Python in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected older assumptions about Cosmos DB's Mongo API lacking vector primitives or confusing Cosmos NoSQL vs the vCore DocumentDB vector features. The new vCore DocumentDB includes integrated vector indexes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no native vector indexes, they may add unnecessary external vector services or implement expensive client-side ANN workarounds. Use the integrated vector index when running vector similarity in-sample to keep queries inside the DB and to reduce operational complexity.
improvements: Document the supported vector index kinds and example createIndex/createIndexes payloads in the agent skill (documentdb-vector-search) and add a short 'How to choose IVF/HNSW/DiskANN' checklist for sample authors.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text and hybrid search for Cosmos DB are typically implemented using Azure Cognitive Search (indexing Cosmos DB documents with an indexer or pushing documents to an Azure Search index). The MongoDB API itself does not have the Atlas Search feature; to get hybrid vector+text search you integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search or an external search engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides an integrated full-text search engine created with createSearchIndexes and queried with a $search aggregation stage (BM25, fuzzy, phrase, custom analyzers). Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector) is supported on the same cluster (server-side RRF or client-side fusion) — both full-text and vector search are integrated and do not require external Azure Cognitive Search.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes + $search)
Hybrid search - combining BM25 and vector with RRF

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older patterns for Cosmos DB used Azure Cognitive Search; the new vCore DocumentDB adds an integrated BM25 search engine and hybrid fusion capabilities which the model did not account for.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes an external search service is required, the sample will become more complex than necessary and may misrepresent DocumentDB capabilities. Prefer the integrated $search + vector approach for the demo.
improvements: Update the 'full-text search' quickstart with a one-page 'hybrid search' example (BM25 + vector) and a code snippet showing server-side RRF via $unionWith so sample authors use the built-in approach by default.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API exposes compatibility with specific MongoDB server versions (historically 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2 and later expanded toward 4.4/5.0 in recent updates). Supported features depend on the chosen server version compatibility level; some advanced MongoDB server features (certain aggregation stages, server-side JavaScript, some change-stream behaviors, $where, and some index types) may be missing or behave differently. My current belief: Cosmos supports many core MongoDB CRUD and aggregation features but not every cutting-edge server feature (and behavior differences exist), so confirm the API compatibility level on your account before relying on very new MongoDB 6/7 features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) documents support MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and implements a high percentage of MongoDB operators (the docs list supported operators and where differences remain). Some administrative or server-level commands are deliberately not exposed in the PaaS service; check the MQL compatibility docs for exact operator support. Change-streams and many aggregation stages are supported in the compatibility matrix.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (overview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious and referenced older compatibility levels; the current docs explicitly list supported mongo wire protocol versions 5.0–8.0 for vCore clusters and enumerate operator support.
confusions.build_risk: Relying on an unsupported new MongoDB server feature without checking the compatibility matrix could cause runtime failures. The builder should consult the compatibility page when choosing aggregation operators or newer MongoDB 8.0-specific features.
improvements: Add a short 'compatibility checklist' at the top of the MQL compatibility page highlighting the most commonly misused features (server-side JS, cluster admin commands, planCache introspection) and recommended alternatives.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (Microsoft-provided). The emulator is primarily a Windows executable, with Linux container images available in preview. The emulator exposes the SQL endpoint on 8081 by default; MongoDB API support in the emulator is limited historically. For full MongoDB-compatible behavior, run a real MongoDB server Docker image locally (e.g., mongo:6.0) listening on the standard MongoDB port 27017 for local tests.
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB development you can run the open-source DocumentDB gateway Docker image locally (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) which exposes the gateway on port 10260. The product docs and quickstarts use the local DocumentDB container and the gateway endpoint at localhost:10260 for MongoDB-compatible connections (with TLS and tlsAllowInvalidCertificates options for local dev).

grounding_links.title: Development loop: Start the DocumentDB container (gateway on port 10260)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the older Cosmos DB emulator story (SQL API emulator) with local DocumentDB gateway options. DocumentDB provides its own local gateway container for Mongo-compatible testing on port 10260.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to use the Cosmos emulator or a plain mongo:latest image for vCore feature parity tests (vector indexes, OIDC), they may not reproduce the service behavior. Use the DocumentDB local gateway container for representative local testing or test against the live cluster as the skill_md instructs.
improvements: Make the 'development-loop' quickstart the single canonical local development doc and add a short table comparing the emulator, mongo:latest, and DocumentDB local gateway (which features each supports).

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams (MongoDB change streams) compatibility depends on the Cosmos DB account's MongoDB API version. Older compatibility tiers did not support change streams; more recent versions may support a subset of change-stream functionality. In many cases nothing special is enabled beyond choosing a MongoDB API compatibility level that supports change streams, but this varies and must be validated for the target account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams (the compatibility docs list $changeStream support for supported server versions). Specific behavior is enumerated in the MQL compatibility documentation; no extra toggle is generally required beyond selecting an API compatibility level that supports change streams.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (shows $changeStream support)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged because older accounts sometimes lacked change-stream support; current vCore clusters support $changeStream in the documented operator matrix.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unsupported could cause the builder to implement a more complex polling solution unnecessarily. Conversely, jumping straight to production-level change-stream reliance without confirming the cluster compatibility level could fail; check the cluster API compatibility level before depending on change streams.
improvements: Add a short 'enablement' note in the compatibility table that calls out any cases where change-streams are not available (for very old compatibility tiers) and how to upgrade a cluster if necessary.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile (the sample environment references a 'documentdb' MCP server). The general Azure MCP server covers ARM/management-plane tasks, but for data-plane inspection (collections, indexes, query plans) use the service-specific 'documentdb' MCP server tooling that speaks MongoDB wire protocol or Cosmos DB management APIs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, sample_documents, aggregate, explain_operation, create_index, etc.). The general Azure MCP server handles control-plane ARM tasks but does not replace the documentdb data-plane toolkit for query/index checks.

grounding_links.title: documentdb

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft's DocumentDB was the original name for the database service that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB is the successor, a multi-model globally distributed database; 'DocumentDB' as a product name is legacy. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB. The MongoDB-compatible interface is an API surface on top of Cosmos DB, not literally the MongoDB server implementation.
confusions.grounded_answer: The cold answer is broadly correct but incomplete for the current vCore product: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore product) was previously offered as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and has been renamed to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility). It is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (the product team publishes docs about the open-source engine). Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Azure Cosmos DB (RU-based) are distinct offerings.

grounding_links.title: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB? (FAQ and history)
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (overview)

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed engine with a MongoDB-compatible API layer. That means applications use MongoDB drivers and most Mongo operations work, but there are semantic and feature differences (throughput billed as RUs, some aggregation or index features missing or different, different consistency semantics). Expect to test critical queries and transactions; in many cases application code is unchanged but edge cases require adaptation.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (published/open-source) built on a PostgreSQL foundation and provides a MongoDB-compatible API layer. Applications use MongoDB drivers with minimal changes, but they must verify feature parity via the compatibility docs. The engine being open-source means you can also run DocumentDB locally or on other clouds if needed.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the older phrase 'proprietary engine' which is misleading for the current vCore product; current docs emphasize the open-source DocumentDB engine powering the service.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a proprietary black-box engine could cause implementers to avoid the local DocumentDB image or open-source operator that would simplify testing and migration. The sample should note the open-source engine and point to the local development container when appropriate.
improvements: Clarify the 'engine' paragraph on the overview page to explain that the vCore product uses DocumentDB open-source, and list the local development options (container, operator) so sample authors can test locally.

confusions.question: Which connection string and environment variable will the sample use at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the Mongo-style connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and pass it directly to the Mongo client (pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'])). The string will be of the form: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<host>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI as specified in the sample run environment. The sample should read DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and pass it to MongoClient. The exact host/format must be taken from the cluster's list-connection-strings output (DOCUMENTDB_URI should contain the correct SRV or host:port string for the vCore cluster).

confusions.question: Which driver and code pattern will the sample use to read data and write the updated price atomically?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo (official MongoDB Python driver). Open a client: client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). Use sessions and transactions: with client.start_session() as s: with s.start_transaction(): product = products.find_one({'_id': prod_id}, session=s); compute new_price; products.update_one({'_id': prod_id}, {'$set': {'price': new_price}}, session=s). This guarantees an atomic read-modify-write for a single-document update and is compatible with MongoDB API compatibility levels that support transactions.
confusions.grounded_answer: Using pymongo with a singleton MongoClient and either a findOneAndUpdate / find_and_modify or a session/transaction for a multi-step atomic operation is the recommended pattern. The quickstarts use pymongo and the DocumentDB compatibility docs indicate multi-document ACID transactions are supported. For a single-document update, find_one_and_update (findAndModify) is atomic and is supported.

confusions.question: How will the sample perform vector similarity if the cluster supports vector indexes (as the environment claims)?
confusions.cold_answer: If the cluster exposes MongoDB 7.x-style vector search, create a vector index on the embedding field using the Mongo createIndex syntax appropriate for the server (e.g., collection.create_index([('embedding', 'knn_vector')], {'type': 'knn', 'm': 16, 'ef': 200}) — adjust params to the provider's syntax). Then query with the provider's vector search operator (e.g., a $vectorSearch or $searchMeta stage). If that syntax isn't accepted, fall back to computing approximate nearest neighbors in-process by calling a separate vector-search service (Azure Cognitive Search custom ANN plugin or an external ANN engine) and then join results with DocumentDB documents.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides native vector indexing (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) and vector search using a cosmosSearch/cosmoSearchOptions index and the $search aggregation stage with cosmosSearch operator. The sample should use the documented createIndex/createIndexes or createSearchIndexes forms and query using $search with the cosmosSearch operator. Fallback to an external ANN is only necessary if the target cluster doesn't have the required vector index kind or tier.

confusions.question: What tooling will the sample use to inspect the live cluster and verify indexes/queries?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server connection profile named default (as provided) to inspect collections, indexes and query plans. For ad-hoc inspection use mongo shell or MongoDB Compass pointed at DOCUMENTDB_URI (with SSL settings). For management-plane verification use az cosmosdb commands (az cosmosdb list-keys, az cosmosdb mongodb list-roles etc.) and the Azure Portal.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is correct in spirit. Use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation, documentdb_aggregate, documentdb_sample_documents) for programmatic verification. For ad-hoc interactive checks you can also use MongoDB Compass or mongosh. For management-plane tasks use az documentdb mongocluster and az CLI commands (not az cosmosdb for vCore clusters).
